(Herrera 2014: 59) ... has a word-stress which occurs on the couplet or on a postcouplet syllable. Word-stress occurs on the first couplet or postcouplet syllable with a tone 1 which is contiguously followed by tone 3. ... (A precouplet syllable never has word-stress even if tone 1. ...) If there is no 13 sequence, word-stress occurs on a syllable with tone 2 of a 23 sequence ... neither the sequence 13, nor 23, word-stress occurs on the first tone 1 of the couplet or postcouplet; if there is no tone 1, then it occurs on the first syllable of the couplet ... Word-stress is predictable by tone provided that the couplet occurs word-initially, but it is not predictable if the couplet occurs elsewhere. new_statements.quote: Si bien el acento de la palabra, siguiendo el parecido de familia, suele estar en la primera mora, los ejemplos anteriores impiden establecer una relación entre el acento y el cierre glotal y con ello alejan la posibilidad de interpretarlo como un rasgo prosódico, ya que habría vocales átonas con cierre glotal y tónicas sin cierre glotal.
new_statements.translation: Although word accent, in keeping with the family resemblance [to other Mixtec languages], usually lies on the first mora, the preceding examples prevent us from establishing a relation between accent and glottal closure, and so rule out interpreting it [the glottal stop] as a prosodic feature, since there would be unstressed vowels with glottal closure and stressed vowels without it.
new_statements.citation: Herrera Zendejas, Esther. 2014. Mapa fónico de las lenguas mexicanas: formas sonoras 1 y 2 (Estudios de Lingüística XIX). México: El Colegio de México, Centro de Estudios Lingüísticos y Literarios. Ch. 2 'Patrones fónicos del mixteco (ISO miy)', pp. 45-75.
new_statements.locator: p. 59 (after Tabla 5 'Función contrastiva del cierre glotal'); supporting context p. 57 ('la palabra es la unidad donde se establecen las distinciones tonales y acentuales... la palabra mínima del mixteco tiene una estructura bimoraica')
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (+.txt, 465 pp., Colmex open repository). At printed p. 59, directly after Tabla 5 'Función contrastiva del cierre glotal' (txt lines 2356-2360), the passage reads exactly as quoted: 'Si bien el acento de la palabra, siguiendo el parecido de familia, suele estar en la primera mora, los ejemplos anteriores impiden establecer una relación entre el acento y el cierre glotal y con ello alejan la posibilidad de interpretarlo como un rasgo prosódico, ya que habría vocales átonas con cierre glotal y tónicas sin cierre glotal.' (only line-break hyphens differ). Supporting context also verified: p. 57 'la palabra es la unidad donde se establecen las distinciones tonales y acentuales... la palab…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ayutla Mixtec is a three-tone language (H, M, L; tone contrastive at word level). The minimal word is a bimoraic couplet and word accent normally falls on its first mora, i.e. root-/couplet-initial stress, as in other Mixtec languages (Herrera Zendejas, own field data from Coscatlán). The fuller primary account (Pankratz & Pike 1967, seen only via de Lacy 2002) makes placement tone-conditioned within the root+suffix domain: leftmost H followed by L, else leftmost H, else leftmost M followed by L, else the leftmost syllable; prefixes and proclitics are never stressed; correlates are duration and raised pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Herrera says nothing about secondary stress; de Lacy 2002 (p. 7), summarising Pankratz & Pike 1967: 'No secondary stress is reported.'
new_statements.exceptions: Herrera hedges with 'suele' (usually) and gives no exceptions; she defers phrase-level accent and its acoustic correlates to future work (p. 75). Pankratz & Pike 1967 (via de Lacy) report stress shifting off the initial syllable onto a later H-toned (or M+L) syllable, including onto enclitics/suffixes, e.g. [kaʔ.iʔ 'ra ri] 'he (man) will eat him (animal)' vs ['kaʔ.iʔ] 'to eat'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: Herrera states the word (bimoraic couplet = minimal word) is the domain of tonal and accentual distinctions; her forms are isolation/citation forms from two speakers of Coscatlán, mun. Ayutla de los Libres. P&P/de Lacy: stress domain = root plus suffixes/enclitics (Prosodic Word), excluding prefixes and proclitics.
new_statements.identity_note: Herrera Zendejas's chapter is explicitly labelled 'Patrones fónicos del mixteco (ISO miy)' and is based on her own recordings of two speakers from Coscatlán, municipio de Ayutla de los Libres, Guerrero (fn. 1, p. 46) — i.e. Ayutla Mixtec, ayut1236. Pankratz & Pike 1967 (seen only second-hand via de Lacy) describe the Ayutla town variety; same glottocode. Not to be confused with Ixtayutla Mixtec (Oaxaca), a different language.

sources.locator: p. 59 (after Tabla 5 'Función contrastiva del cierre glotal'); supporting context p. 57 ('la palabra es la unidad donde se establecen las distinciones tonales y acentuales... la palabra mínima del mixteco tiene una estructura bimoraica')
sources.note: p.57: the word is the unit where tonal and accentual distinctions are established; minimal word is bimoraic (couplet). p.59: word accent, following the family resemblance, usually lies on the first mora, but glottal closure is contrastive and independent of accent (unstressed vowels can bear it, stressed ones lack it). p.75 conclusion: phrase-level accent and its acoustic correlates left for future study. Chapter is otherwise about segments, glottalization and tone (3 tones, downstep, tonal inversion).

sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew K. 2016. Phonological Typology (Oxford). Sec. 6.6 (tone-sensitive stress, Ayutla Mixtec) — only sec. 6.7 excerpt held locally.
sources.note: Sec. 6.7 p.: 'The tone-sensitive stress system of Ayutla Mixtec (section 6.6) also draws a distinction between suffixes, which are part of the stress domain, and prefixes which are not.' Section 6.6 itself not held. Second-hand (from Pankratz & Pike via de Lacy).

sources.citation: de Lacy, Paul. 2002. The interaction of tone and stress in Optimality Theory. Phonology 19(1): 1-32. doi:10.1017/S0952675702004220 (author postprint).
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 (pp. 5-7), restating Pankratz & Pike 1967 with their page refs: stress falls on roots or suffixes, never prefixes/proclitics (P&P p.292); tone-driven placement within root+suffix domain: (a) leftmost H-toned syllable immediately followed by L; (b) else leftmost H; (c) else leftmost M followed by L; (d) else leftmost syllable (all-L or all-M words are initial-stressed); correlates are greater duration and higher pitch (P&P pp. 289, 294); 'No secondary stress is reported'; single left-aligned trochaic foot per PrWd. Second-hand.
